stem: Which of the following is a risk factor for severe bronchiolitis?
explanation: Severe bronchiolitis is associated with several recognised risk factors, including prematurity, young age, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, exposure to tobacco smoke, and childcare attendance. Because multiple listed options are true, the best single answer here is the most directly stated source option, prematurity.

citations.title: Practice Quiz: Emergency Medicine - Breathing difficulties

rationale: The source item is ambiguous because several options are medically true. Under select-if-possible, the best available preserved answer is the source-emphasised option, prematurity.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Prematurity is a recognised risk factor for severe bronchiolitis.
optionExplanations.B: Also a risk factor, but not the best single answer in this preserved item.
optionExplanations.C: Also a recognised risk factor for severe bronchiolitis.
optionExplanations.D: Also increases risk of severe bronchiolitis.
optionExplanations.E: Also associated with increased risk due to exposure to other children and viral spread.
optionExplanations.F: Incorrect because the item is not intended to have multiple correct answers.

Which of the following is a risk factors for severe bronchiolitis?

Prematurity (gestational age <37 weeks)

Instructions

The following nine questions refer to Patrick’s clinical scenario.

Clinical scenario 1 - Patrick

Patrick, a six month old infant, is brought to the emergency department with wheezing and respiratory distress. On examination he has severe chest wall retractions, grunting and is pale. His vital signs are:

RR 80/min, HR 190/min, temperature 38.0’C, SaO2 80% in room air.

The accompanying table has the normal ranges indicated in the 2010 NSW Health Standard Paediatric Observation Chart, SPOC.

Patrick has wheeze and crackles throughout his chest. There is a history of having been snuffly with a cough for the last two days. The entire family has a cold.
